task_row_model.query: A 58-year-old patient presents with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) 9 hours after chest pain onset. Is fibrinolytic therapy indicated, and what contraindications would preclude its use?

documents.content: Clinical guideline excerpt (academic tone): Current reperfusion guidance emphasizes primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as preferred for STEMI when it can be performed promptly. If PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact, fibrinolytic therapy is recommended when symptom onset is within 12 hours. The guideline notes efficacy declines after 12 hours and bleeding risk rises. Historical discussion about early streptokinase trials and evolution of protocols is included as background but is not prescriptive for current timing recommendations.

Journalistic rapid-summary for emergency clinicians: Absolute contraindications to fibrinolytic therapy are listed clearly to prevent catastrophic hemorrhage. These include any prior intracranial hemorrhage at any time, ischemic stroke within the previous 3 months, suspected aortic dissection, active internal bleeding, and recent intracranial surgery or head trauma within 3 months. The piece also offers loosely related statistics about national fibrinolysis use rates and an unrelated case study of hemorrhagic conversion after thrombolysis as cautionary anecdote.

Pocket-reference note (concise, directive style): Use fibrinolytics for STEMI presenting within 12 hours when PCI unavailable within 120 minutes. Before giving fibrinolysis, check for other exclusions: uncontrolled blood pressure (systolic >180 mmHg or diastolic >110 mmHg) and recent major surgery are considered important contraindications to address; many references cite recent major non-cranial surgery within 3 weeks as a relative or absolute exclusion depending on bleeding risk. The card includes definitional boilerplate about dosing and monitoring and speculative commentary on risk–benefit in elderly patients.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Fibrinolysis is indicated for STEMI presenting within 12 hours if primary PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes. Absolute contraindications that preclude fibrinolysis include prior intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke within 3 months, suspected aortic dissection, active internal bleeding, and intracranial surgery or head trauma within 3 months. Uncontrolled BP >180/110 and recent major surgery (within ~3 weeks) are important contraindications to correct or consider before treatment.
